content: Offline-First Android Architecture: The Complete Engineering Guide Ashutosh Kumar 9 min read · 3 days ago -- Listen Share How to design Android apps that treat the network as an optimization layer, not a requirement Press enter or click to view image in full size Introduction Mobile users open apps from basements, trains, elevators, flights, and rural areas with patchy signal. Despite that, most Android apps are still built on a fragile assumption: that the network is always there. The moment a request times out, the whole experience collapses into spinners and error screens. Offline-first architecture flips this assumption. Instead of the network being the source of truth, your local database becomes the source of truth , and the network becomes a background synchronization mechanism. The UI never waits on a socket — it reads from Room, updates instantly, and lets sync happen quietly underneath. This guide walks through the full system: architecture patterns, sync strategies, conflict resolution, caching, retention, edge cases, and testing. Part 1 — Why Offline-First The problem with traditional (network-first) architecture In a typical app, the UI asks a repository for data, the repository hits an API, and the UI waits. If the request fails — weak signal, timeout, disconnection — the whole flow breaks down into an error screen and a retry button. The core flaw is treating the network as the single source of truth: one dropped socket can make the entire app feel unusable. Press enter or click to view image in full size The offline-first flip Press enter or click to view image in full size The paradigm shift, visually Press enter or click to view image in full size Part 2 — Core Architecture Patterns The Repository Pattern The repository is the gatekeeper between your domain logic and your data sources. In offline-first apps, it orchestrates the dance between local storage and the remote API — reads always come from Room, writes always go to Room first. Press enter or click to view image in full size // The key insight: UI always observes the local database. // Network operations write to the local database. // UI updates reactively from database changes. interface ArticleRepository { fun observeArticles(): Flow<List<Article>> fun observeArticle(id: String): Flow<Article?> suspend fun refreshArticles(): Result<Unit> suspend fun createArticle(article: Article): Result<Article> suspend fun updateArticle(article: Article): Result<Article> suspend fun deleteArticle(id: String): Result<Unit> } Single Source of Truth (SSOT) Press enter or click to view image in full size The Outbox Pattern For write operations, the outbox pattern guarantees no data is lost while offline — the write goes to the entity table and an outbox table in the same local transaction; a background worker drains the outbox whenever connectivity allows. Press enter or click to view image in full size // Outbox entity for pending operations @Entity(tableName = "outbox") data class OutboxEntry( @PrimaryKey val id: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString(), val entityType: String,      // "article", "comment", etc. val entityId: String,        // ID of the affected entity val operation: Operation,    // CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE val payload: String,         // JSON serialized data val createdAt: Long = System.currentTimeMillis(), val retryCount: Int = 0, val lastError: String? = null ) enum class Operation { CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE } Part 3 — Data Synchronization Strategies Full sync vs. incremental sync Approach How it works Trade-off Full Sync Fetch all data, replace local Simple logic, high bandwidth Incremental Sync Track last sync time, fetch only changes, merge with local Low bandwidth, more moving parts Hybrid Initial full sync, subsequent incremental, periodic full refresh Best of both — most production apps land here Incremental sync in practice Press enter or click to view image in full size Sync token strategies Strategy How it works Pros Cons Timestamp lastModified > ? Simple Clock skew issues Cursor/Token Opaque server token Server controls pagination Requires server support Version Vector Per-entity versions Precise Complex to implement Event Sourcing Sequential event IDs Complete history Storage heavy Bidirectional sync flow Press enter or click to view image in full size Sync priority rules worth following: User-generated content (posts, edits, comments) gets immediate sync with aggressive retry — it should never be silently lost. Low-value telemetry (read receipts, view counts) can sync lazily and fail silently under poor connectivity. Operations on the same entity must preserve order — a create followed by an edit must reach the server in that sequence, enforced via sequence numbers or timestamps. On reconnect, wait 2–5 seconds before syncing — mobile radios often flicker on/off before stabilizing. Batch related operations instead of firing dozens of individual requests. Part 4 — Conflict Resolution Conflicts happen when the same record is modified on two devices before they sync. This isn’t an edge case in offline-first systems — it’s the normal case. title: Classes and Objects in Kotlin: A Complete Beginner’s Guide
excerpt: Imagine you’re building an e-commerce app. Every product has a name, price, category, and stock quantity. Customers have names, email… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Classes and Objects in Kotlin: A Complete Beginner’s Guide Tech Dynasty 5 min read · 3 days ago -- Listen Share Imagine you’re building an e-commerce app. Every product has a name, price, category, and stock quantity. Customers have names, email addresses, and shipping addresses. Orders contain products, payment details, and delivery status. These are all real-world entities with their own data and behavior. How do we represent them in code? The answer is Classes and Objects . Press enter or click to view image in full size Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is one of the core paradigms of Kotlin and Android development. Classes and objects allow us to model real-world concepts, organize code logically, and build scalable applications. In this article, you’ll learn everything you need to know about classes and objects in Kotlin, from the basics to practical Android examples. What Is a Class? A class is a blueprint or template used to create objects. Think of a class as the architectural drawing of a house. The blueprint defines: Number of rooms Doors Windows Layout But it isn’t an actual house. Similarly, a Kotlin class defines: Properties (data) Functions (behavior) without creating actual objects. What Is an Object? An object is an actual instance of a class. If a class is a blueprint, an object is the house built from that blueprint. For example: Blueprint: Car Objects: BMW Tesla Toyota Honda Every car shares common characteristics but has different values. Creating Your First Class Let’s create a simple Student class. class Student This class doesn’t contain any data or behavior yet. Now let’s create an object. val student = Student() The parentheses call the class constructor and create a new object. Properties Properties store the state (data) of an object. Example: class Student { var name = "" var age = 0 } Creating an object: val student = Student() student.name = "Janhvi" student.age = 24 println(student.name) println(student.age) Output: Janhvi 24 Here: name age are properties of the Student class. Functions Inside a Class Classes can also define behavior. class Student { var name = "" fun study() { println("$name is studying.") } } Usage: val student = Student() student.name = "Alex" student.study() Output: Alex is studying. Primary Constructor Instead of declaring properties separately, Kotlin lets you define them directly in the constructor. class Student( var name: String, var age: Int ) Creating an object: val student = Student( "Janhvi", 24 ) This is the most common way to create classes in Kotlin. Read-Only Properties Use val when a property should never change. class User( val id: Int, var name: String ) The user’s ID remains constant, while the name can be updated. Default Values Constructors can provide default values. class Product( var name: String = "Unknown", var price: Double = 0.0 ) Now you can create: val product = Product() or val product = Product( "Laptop", 65000.0 ) This makes object creation flexible and reduces boilerplate. The init Block Sometimes you need to execute code when an object is created. Kotlin provides the init block. class User( val name: String ) { init { println("User Created: $name") } } Whenever a new object is created, the init block runs automatically. This is useful for validation and initialization. Multiple Objects One class can create many objects. val student1 = Student( "Alex", 22 ) val student2 = Student( "Rahul", 24 ) Both objects share the same structure but hold different data. This is one of the biggest strengths of object-oriented programming. Member Functions Functions defined inside a class are called member functions . Example: class BankAccount( var balance: Double ) { fun deposit(amount: Double) { balance += amount } fun withdraw(amount: Double) { balance -= amount } } Usage: val account = BankAccount(1000.0) account.deposit(500.0) println(account.balance) Output: 1500.0 Accessing Properties Properties are accessed using the dot ( . ) operator. val product = Product() product.name = "Keyboard" println(product.name) This syntax is simple and highly readable. Nested Classes A class can contain another class. class University { class Student } Creating an object: val student = University.Student() Nested classes help group related functionality. Real-World Android Example Imagine an e-commerce application. class Product( val id: Int, val name: String, val price: Double, var stock: Int ) { fun purchase(quantity: Int) { stock -= quantity } } Usage: val product = Product( 101, "Wireless Mouse", 999.0, 20 ) product.purchase(2) println(product.stock) Output: 18 This closely resembles the type of classes you’ll write in Android applications. Another Example: User Profile class User( val id: Int, var name: String, var email: String ) { fun displayProfile() { println("ID: $id") println("Name: $name") println("Email: $email") } } Objects: val user = User( 1, "Janhvi", "janhvi@example.com" ) user.displayProfile() Why Classes Matter in Android Development Almost everything in Android is based on classes. Examples include: Activity Fragment ViewModel Repository Room Database RecyclerView.Adapter Worker Service Whenever you create a screen or a data model, you’re creating a class. Understanding classes is essential for writing scalable Android applications. Best Practices When creating Kotlin classes: Give classes meaningful names. Keep each class focused on a single responsibility. Prefer immutable ( val ) properties whenever possible. Use constructors to initialize required data. Keep member functions small and focused. Avoid storing unrelated data in the same class. Following these practices makes your code easier to understand and maintain. title: Goodbye, cw-json! Hello, kPointer!
excerpt: The cw-json project has been replaced by kPointer -- learn what kPointer offers!
content: Goodbye, cw-json! Hello, kPointer! I have supplanted cw-json , replacing it with a new library, kPointer . The concept is the same, and porting from cw-json to kPointer is fairly straightforward. However, I realized that I made a key mistake when I started cw-json: thinking that I was only dealing with JSON. (naming things is hard) More Object Types kPointer not only supports extracting values from JSON by means of JSON Pointer paths, as cw-json did. kPointer also supports YAML (by way of yamlkt) and HTML/XML (by way of Ksoup). All get wrapped by an adapter-style abstraction layer, and you can make custom adapters to support other object tree structures. Part of the reason for supporting YAML, HTML, and XML was to exercise the abstraction layer. I am a firm believer in the “rule of 3” when it comes to APIs, frameworks, and abstraction layers: you need at least 3 separate implementations to feel comfortable that what you have will be able to handle more beyond those 3. If you happen to want to adapt other structures, there is a conformance test suite that you can leverage as the basis for your own tests to see if your implementation covers all the cases. Personally, I am anticipating adding support for other data structures in the not-too-distant future. A Better “Dot Notation” Option The final release of cw-json, 0.4.0 , introduced support for an ad-hoc sort of “dot notation” syntax, alongside JSON Pointer and its kin (relative JSON Pointer, JSON Pointer fragment syntax). “Dot notation” was aiming at the syntax that you see in template languages like Handlebars or Mustache, such as foo.bar.goo , to navigate into an object graph. kPointer replaces that ad-hoc dot notation with… well, OK, a better ad-hoc dot notation, what I’m calling JavaScript access path notation . This is pretty much a clean superset of the original dot notation, but also supports bracket syntax (e.g., foo['bar'] or foo[0] ). Porting Support Since I am anticipating porting kPointer to other languages in the future, I have a fairly extensive conformance suite , as part of broader support for porting kPointer. kPointer comes with a CLI designed for running the conformance suite, and ports could create their own workalike CLI to assist in testing. A Dedicated Site Whereas cw-json had a long README and not much more, kPointer has a dedicated site , with lots of information on using the libraries and more. What’s Next? As I mentioned earlier, I expect to be adding support for more data format parsers, covering more data formats. For example, I expect to be adding support for CSV and similar delimited file formats. It’s possible that I will add more pointer syntaxes besides the flavors of JSON Pointer and JavaScript access paths. I do not have any current plans in that area, but, hey, plans change. — Jul 22, 2026

content: RustRover Focus on what matters Follow Follow: X X Download All News Releases Backend Features RustRover Axum Support in RustRover 2026.2: Build Web Backends Faster Tatiana Parshutkina Axum support, one of the most popular web frameworks in the Rust ecosystem, is one of the highlights of the RustRover 2026.2 release . If you’re building web services, APIs, or distributed systems in Rust, this update makes it easier to navigate routes, understand request flows, and generate client calls directly from the IDE. Let’s take a closer look at why web development has become an important Rust use case, what makes Axum popular, and how RustRover can help you work with it more efficiently. Why use Rust for web backend development? For many years, Rust was primarily associated with systems programming, embedded development, and performance-critical infrastructure. While these remain important areas, the language has expanded into backend and web development. According to the Developer Ecosystem 2025 survey report, building web backends with Rust is the third most-popular use case, showing that Rust is increasingly trusted for building services and APIs. This shift matters because backend systems are often long-lived and business-critical, so this application of Rust signals confidence in its stability and ecosystem support. Rust isn’t filling in the backend the same space as Node.js or Django. It appears where the stakes are high: in infrastructure APIs, data processing pipelines, high-throughput microservices, edge computing, and security-sensitive services, where memory safety bugs can have serious consequences. The Rust ecosystem offers several mature web frameworks and libraries, each with its own strengths: Actix Web is known for its performance and mature ecosystem. Rocket focuses on developer-friendly APIs and conventions. warp emphasizes composable filters and type-safe routing. Poem provides simplicity with built-in OpenAPI support. Axum emphasizes ergonomics and modularity for HTTP routing and request handling. Among them, Axum has emerged as one of the most widely adopted choices thanks to its ergonomic design, modular architecture, and seamless Tokio integration. Its popularity is reflected in more than 850K daily downloads on crates.io and over 25K GitHub stars. What is Axum? Axum is an HTTP routing and request-handling library that focuses on ergonomics and modularity. It is maintained by the Tokio team – the same people behind Rust’s most widely used async runtime – and that shows in the design. Axum builds on the infrastructure the Rust async ecosystem already has, and gets out of the way. At a high level, Axum lets you: Route requests to handlers with a macro-free API – no #[get(“/”) ] decorators, just plain Rust functions. Declaratively parse requests using extractors, with compile-time validation of path parameters, query strings, and request bodies. Apply a simple and predictable error handling model that keeps error paths explicit. Generate responses with minimal boilerplate. Take full advantage of the Tower and tower-http ecosystem of middleware, services, and utilities. That last point is what sets Axum apart from other frameworks. Axum doesn’t have its own middleware system – it uses tower::Service directly. This means Axum gets timeouts, tracing, compression, rate limiting, and authorization for free, just by pulling in Tower middleware. It also means middleware can be shared across applications built with hyper or Tonic – the wider Tokio ecosystem is your ecosystem. Axum is designed to work with Tokio and hyper . Runtime and transport layer independence is not a goal at present, which keeps the design focused and the integration tight. You can learn more in the documentation . Axum in production Axum adoption spans commercial infrastructure and open-source tooling alike. The official Rust package registry, crates.io , runs on Axum. It is one of the highest-profile Rust web applications in existence, and it serves the entire Rust community on every cargo build . Cloudflare Workers support Axum directly through the workers-rs crate, allowing developers to write Cloudflare edge functions using the same Axum routing model they use in standard services. Beyond these examples, Axum has become the recommended foundation for several Rust web stacks and starter templates. Loco , the Rails-inspired Rust framework, is built on top of Axum. It is also heavily used in production by Lichess for several of their core background services and microservices. Axum is increasingly the default answer when someone asks, “How do I build a web service in Rust?” Navigate Axum routes and generate Reqwest calls faster In Axum projects, route strings are the entry points to your service, but tracing them back to handlers, or related client calls, often still means searching through the code manually. RustRover 2026.2 introduces support for the Axum and Reqwest libraries. This release also adds Reqwest support with request generation and navigation features, helping you create client calls with less manual setup. content: Android AI Mobile App Development From Cloud LLM to On-Device Whisper: Turning Speech into Structured Actions on Android Stevan Milovanovic 8 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size In two earlier articles I looked at the same idea from opposite ends. In Building AI features on Android with Firebase AI Logic , I built a voice feature where the app captures audio, sends it to Firebase AI Logic, and Gemini returns a structured output that maps directly to an app action. It worked nicely, but I also called out where that approach is not the best fit: sensitive data, fully offline use, and long-term usage-based pricing. In Exploring On-Device AI for Android , I went the other way and ran models directly on the device (image classification, captioning, a small LLM) using high-level Google SDKs like LiteRT and MediaPipe . This article joins those two threads. I took the voice use case from the first article and rebuilt it fully on-device, but one level lower than the second: transcription runs on a vendored C/C++ engine ( whisper.cpp ) through JNI, and the reasoning step is a plain, deterministic Kotlin parser instead of an LLM. A quick honesty note up front: this is an exploration and a learning exercise, not a production blueprint. I don’t have much NDK/C++ experience, so I leaned on AI assistance for the native glue (the JNI bridge and CMake setup). The part I’ll focus on, is the Kotlin and architecture side. The Use Case The goal is the same as in the Firebase article. A user says something like: “Send Maria 10 euros for the taxi.” …and the app turns it into a structured, machine-readable intent it can act on: data class ParsedVoiceTransaction( val action: VoiceTransactionAction,   // SEND or REQUEST val amount: BigDecimal, val receiverName: String, val currency: String? = null,         // normalized ISO code, e.g. "EUR" val message: String? = null,          // the verbatim reason, e.g. "for the taxi" ) Previously, Gemini produced that structure in the cloud. Now I wanted the same result with nothing leaving the device. Two design decisions Moving on-device came down to two choices. Transcription runs locally with Whisper. Whisper is OpenAI’s speech-recognition model — a transformer trained on a lot of audio. whisper.cpp is a small, dependency-free C/C++ runtime for it (built on the ggml tensor library) that runs on the CPU. So yes, this is genuinely “on-device AI”; the model just happens to be executed by native code instead of a Google SDK. I use a quantized tiny model (~42 MB), which is the realistic size/quality trade-off for a phone. The “reasoning” step becomes a deterministic parser. In the cloud version, the LLM did double duty: it transcribed and inferred the structured fields. On-device, Whisper gave me only a transcript. Turning that transcript into a structured data was done by rules, not a model. That second decision is a real trade-off, and I want to be honest about it: An LLM handles phrasing variety gracefully (“pass Maria a tenner for the cab”) but is non-deterministic and, in the cloud case, needs a network call. A rule-based parser is deterministic, instant, testable, and free — but I own the grammar, and it’s brittle to phrasings I didn’t anticipate. For something as sensitive as a payment intent, I actually want the predictable, unit-testable option. Architecture overview The flow is a straight pipeline, and it’s all ordinary Kotlin except for one native hop: Press enter or click to view image in full size Architecture Overview Diagram The key detail is that I kept the same interface from the Firebase AI Logic implementation. Both versions hide behind SpeechToTransactionService . In the cloud version the implementation talked to Firebase. Here, a WhisperSpeechToTransactionService downloads the model, transcribes, and parses. The ViewModel and UI never know which one they’re using — Hilt binds the implementation. That interface boundary is what made swapping the whole approach a contained change rather than a rewrite. Whisper as a black box I’ll be honest, I treat whisper.cpp as a black box. The engine is vendored open-source code (v1.7.6), and the JNI bridge that exposes it to Kotlin was written with the help of AI. Get Stevan Milovanovic ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. title: Constructors in Kotlin: Primary, Secondary Constructors, and init Blocks Explained
excerpt: Whenever you create an object in Kotlin, something important happens behind the scenes — the object is initialized. Properties receive… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Kotlin Beginners Android Software Development Software Engineering Constructors in Kotlin: Primary, Secondary Constructors, and init Blocks Explained Tech Dynasty 5 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share Whenever you create an object in Kotlin, something important happens behind the scenes — the object is initialized. Properties receive their initial values, validation logic may run, and setup code is executed before the object is ready to use. Constructors are responsible for this entire process. Press enter or click to view image in full size Whether you’re creating a User , Product , Order , or ViewModel , understanding constructors is essential for writing clean and reliable Kotlin applications. In this article, you’ll learn everything you need to know about constructors in Kotlin, including primary constructors, secondary constructors, init blocks, constructor delegation, and real-world Android examples. What Is a Constructor? A constructor is a special part of a class that is executed when an object is created. Its primary purpose is to initialize the object with the required data. For example: class User( val name: String, val age: Int ) Creating an object: val user = User("Janhvi", 24) Here, the constructor initializes the name and age properties. Without constructors, you would need to create an object first and then manually assign every property. Why Do We Need Constructors? Imagine an e-commerce application. Every product must have: Product ID Name Price Instead of writing: val product = Product() product.id = 101 product.name = "Laptop" product.price = 65000.0 You can ensure every product is created with valid information. val product = Product( 101, "Laptop", 65000.0 ) Constructors help create complete, valid objects from the beginning. Primary Constructor The primary constructor is the most common type of constructor in Kotlin. It is declared directly after the class name. class Student( val name: String, val age: Int ) Creating an object: val student = Student( "Alex", 21 ) The constructor automatically initializes the properties. Primary Constructor with var and val Constructor parameters become properties only when marked with val or var . class Employee( val id: Int, var department: String ) val creates a read-only property. var creates a mutable property. Constructor Without Properties Sometimes constructor parameters are only needed during initialization. class Circle(radius: Double) { val area = 3.14 * radius * radius } Here, radius is used to calculate the area but isn't stored as a property. Default Parameter Values Kotlin allows default values in constructors. class Product( val name: String = "Unknown", val price: Double = 0.0 ) Now all of these are valid: val p1 = Product() val p2 = Product("Keyboard") val p3 = Product("Laptop", 65000.0) Default values reduce the need for multiple overloaded constructors. The init Block Sometimes initialization requires more than assigning values. Kotlin provides the init block, which runs immediately after the primary constructor. class User( val name: String ) { init { println("User created: $name") } } Creating an object: val user = User("Janhvi") Output: User created: Janhvi The init block is commonly used for validation and setup logic. Validating Data with init class User( val age: Int ) { init { require(age >= 18) { "Age must be at least 18." } } } Usage: val user = User(16) Output: IllegalArgumentException: Age must be at least 18. Using require() helps ensure invalid objects are never created. Multiple init Blocks A class can have multiple init blocks. class Example( val name: String ) { init { println("First init block") } init { println("Second init block") } } They execute in the order they appear. Although possible, using a single init block is usually easier to read. Secondary Constructors Sometimes a class needs multiple ways to create objects. Secondary constructors are declared using the constructor keyword. class Student { var name = "" var age = 0 constructor() { println("Default constructor") } constructor(name: String, age: Int) { this.name = name this.age = age } } Usage: val student1 = Student() val student2 = Student("Alex", 22) Secondary constructors are less common than primary constructors but are useful in specific situations. Constructor Delegation If a class has both a primary and secondary constructor, every secondary constructor must delegate to the primary constructor. class Product( val name: String ) { constructor() : this("Unknown") } Here, the secondary constructor calls the primary constructor using this() . This ensures all initialization logic runs consistently. Combining Primary Constructor and init class Employee( val name: String, val salary: Double ) { init { println("$name earns ₹$salary") } } Creating an object: val employee = Employee( "Rahul", 50000.0 ) Output: Rahul earns ₹50000.0 Real-World Android Examples User Model class User( val id: Int, val name: String, val email: String ) Every user object starts with complete information. Product Validation class Product( val name: String, val price: Double ) { init { require(price >= 0) { "Price cannot be negative." } } } This prevents invalid product objects from being created. Database Entity class Order( val orderId: Int, val amount: Double, val status: String = "Pending" ) Using default values keeps object creation concise. Primary vs Secondary Constructors Press enter or click to view image in full size In most Kotlin projects, you’ll primarily use primary constructors with default values , reserving secondary constructors for cases where multiple initialization paths are genuinely required. Best Practices When designing Kotlin classes: Prefer primary constructors whenever possible. Use val for immutable properties and var only when values need to change. Use default parameter values instead of creating many secondary constructors. Keep init blocks focused on validation or initialization logic. Use require() and check() to v

title: Google’s Android XR Is Here: Here’s What Developers Need to Know
excerpt: From spatial multitasking on headsets to glanceable HUDs on smart glasses, spatial computing is officially coming to the Android ecosystem. Continue reading on ProAndroidDev »
content: Google’s Android XR Is Here: Here’s What Developers Need to Know Pankaj Rai 🇮🇳 4 min read · 1 day ago -- 1 Listen Share From spatial multitasking on headsets to glanceable HUDs on smart glasses, spatial computing is officially coming to the Android ecosystem. Press enter or click to view image in full size Spatial computing is shifting from a futuristic promise into everyday reality. With Android XR , Google is expanding the Android ecosystem beyond smartphones, tablets and wearables directly into extended reality (XR). Whether you are an Android developer looking to port your existing app or a 3D creator building the next immersive game, here is a quick breakdown of what Android XR brings to the table. One Platform, Multiple Forms of Hardware Unlike platforms built for a single device, Android XR is designed as a unified operating system for a wide hardware spectrum: XR Headsets & Wired Glasses (for deeply immersive, high-fidelity experiences) Display & Audio Glasses (for lightweight, ambient everyday assistance) Two Core Experience Categories Android XR breaks down app experiences into two distinct modes depending on the user’s hardware: Immersive Experiences: Designed for headsets and tethered glasses. These allow users to float multi-window Android apps in 3D space, anchor digital objects to physical tables or fully transport themselves into virtual environments. Augmented Experiences: Designed for sleek, everyday smart glasses. Instead of filling your field of view, these experiences deliver lightweight context — like turn-by-turn navigation, real-time language translation or quick hands-free AI voice interactions. Immersive Experiences (Headsets & Wired XR Glasses) Immersive experiences are designed for hardware like standalone XR headsets or tethered glasses. They blur the lines between virtual and physical environments or replace the real world entirely. 1. Home Space vs Full Space At the heart of the spatial OS interface are two modes of operation: Home Space (Spatial Multitasking): Your app lives inside a spatial window alongside other 2D and 3D app panels. Users can position, resize and multitask across multiple app windows floating in their real-world environment. Full Space (Full Spatial Takeover): When the user triggers an action requiring total focus — like starting a game or opening a 3D CAD canvas — your app transitions into Full Space . The app takes over the entire virtual environment, unlocking unbound 3D coordinates. Android XR allows apps to smoothly transition between Home Space and Full Space whenever the context calls for it. 2. Spatial UI with Jetpack Compose for XR You don’t need to learn a complex game engine just to add spatial depth to an app UI. Jetpack Compose for XR introduces declarative spatial primitives: Spatial Panels: Transform standard 2D layouts into floating 3D windows. Depth & Elevation: Add spatial z-index depth to standard UI components. Spatial Environments & Entities: Embed 3D models (GLTF/USDZ), stereoscopic 3D videos, or full 360-degree virtual skyboxes directly into your Jetpack Compose scene. Augmented Experiences (AI Display & Audio Glasses) While headsets prioritize depth and presence, smart glasses prioritize weight, battery life and all-day wearability . Android XR introduces a dedicated sub-framework designed exclusively for ambient display and audio glasses. Jetpack Compose Glimmer Standard mobile UI components don’t work on tiny micro-displays. To solve this, Google introduced Jetpack Compose Glimmer — a purpose-built UI toolkit optimized for display glasses. Micro-UI Design: Features high-contrast, minimalist and glanceable UI elements optimized for small fields of view. All-Day Comfort: Prioritizes low-latency rendering and minimal battery consumption so users can wear glasses comfortably all day. 2. Conversational AI with the Gemini Live API Smart glasses thrive on multimodal input. Android XR natively integrates the Gemini Live API for conversational, context-aware AI experiences: Voice-First Interaction: Users talk to your app naturally, bypassing the need for touch controls. Contextual Awareness: Glasses leverage camera feed data and audio queues to let Gemini “see and hear” what the user is experiencing in real-time. Build with the Tools You Already Know The biggest win for developers is accessibility. You don’t need to learn a completely new paradigm from scratch: For Android Devs (Jetpack XR SDK): If you know Kotlin and Jetpack Compose , you can build spatial apps today. Existing 2D Android apps can automatically run as floating spatial panels, which you can then enhance with 3D elements and spatial layouts. For 3D & Game Devs: Android XR offers native support for Unity, Godot, Unreal Engine and OpenXR standards. For Web Devs: Native support for WebXR brings spatial web apps directly into the ecosystem. No XR Headset? No Problem. You don’t need expensive test hardware to start building. Google has built the Android XR Emulator directly into Android Studio. It allows you to simulate hand gestures, eye gaze tracking, spatial layouts and environment lighting directly on your desktop. Spatial computing doesn’t have to mean fragmented ecosystems or starting your codebase from zero. Android XR leverages the massive existing Android developer ecosystem to make building spatial experiences fast, familiar, and accessible.

content: Navigation 3: Keep entryProvider from Becoming a Giant Switchboard chanzmao 7 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share Organize Related Screens with EntryProviderScope Press enter or click to view image in full size Image created by AI One of the first things you’ll probably do when adopting Navigation 3 is register every destination directly inside entryProvider . For small projects, that’s a perfectly reasonable place to start. NavDisplay( backStack = backStack, entryProvider = entryProvider { entry<HomeRoute> { HomeScreen() } entry<DetailRoute> { DetailScreen() } entry<LoginRoute> { LoginScreen() } entry<SignupRoute> { SignupScreen() } entry<SettingsRoute> { SettingsScreen() } entry<LicenseRoute> { LicenseScreen() } } ) At this stage, the navigation structure is easy to understand. Every destination is visible in one place, and adding a new screen simply means adding another entry() . The problem is that applications rarely stay this small. As features evolve, more screens are introduced. Authentication gains password recovery and email verification. Settings grow into multiple sections. Checkout flows become more sophisticated. Onboarding expands as the product matures. Without noticing it, entryProvider slowly turns into the place that knows about every destination in your application. Eventually, you’ll start seeing familiar symptoms. entryProvider grows into hundreds of lines. It’s difficult to see which screens belong to which feature. Feature modules become harder to separate. Every new screen requires editing the application’s root navigation. Multiple developers frequently modify the same file, increasing merge conflicts. None of these problems are caused by Navigation 3 itself. They’re simply a consequence of putting every destination into a single location. The file may still compile just fine, but it gradually stops representing your application’s architecture. Instead of describing how features fit together, it becomes a giant switchboard responsible for wiring every screen together. Extract Features with EntryProviderScope Instead of registering every destination in one place, group related screens into an extension function on EntryProviderScope<NavKey> . For example, an authentication feature can be written like this. fun EntryProviderScope<NavKey>.authFeature( onAuthSuccess: () -> Unit, onNavigateToSignup: () -> Unit, onBack: () -> Unit ) { entry<LoginRoute> { LoginScreen( onLoginSuccess = onAuthSuccess, onSignupClick = onNavigateToSignup ) } entry<SignupRoute> { SignupScreen( onSignupSuccess = onAuthSuccess, onBackClick = onBack ) } } At first glance, this looks like nothing more than a Kotlin extension function. And that’s exactly the point. Navigation 3 doesn’t introduce another navigation abstraction to replace navigation() . Instead, it lets ordinary Kotlin functions become the unit of organization. Rather than exposing two independent screens, authFeature() exposes a single feature. The implementation details stay inside that function, while the rest of the application only interacts with the feature itself. This is a subtle shift, but it’s one of the biggest architectural differences between Navigation 2 and Navigation 3. Why This Fits Navigation 3 Better One of Navigation 3’s design goals is to embrace Compose instead of building another layer of navigation-specific APIs. Compose encourages us to build UIs by composing small, reusable functions. Navigation 3 follows the same philosophy. Instead of composing UI elements, we’re composing navigation features. That means your navigation structure can be expressed using familiar Kotlin constructs instead of a dedicated graph DSL. Your navigation code becomes easier to refactor because features are simply functions. They’re easy to move into separate files. They’re easy to place inside feature modules. They’re easy to review because each function has a clear responsibility. Most importantly, they scale naturally as the application grows. The Root Navigation Only Composes Features Once destinations are grouped into features, the application’s root navigation becomes dramatically smaller. NavDisplay( backStack = backStack, entryProvider = entryProvider { homeFeature() detailFeature( onBackClick = onBack ) authFeature( onAuthSuccess = { onNavigate(HomeRoute) }, onNavigateToSignup = { onNavigate(SignupRoute) }, onBack = onBack ) settingsFeature() paymentFeature() } ) Notice how little the root navigation actually knows. It doesn’t know how many authentication screens exist. It doesn’t know whether password recovery was added last week. It doesn’t know whether onboarding was expanded from three screens to six. Instead, it simply declares that the application contains an authentication feature, a settings feature, a payment feature, and so on. That’s a much higher level of abstraction. The application’s entry point focuses on composing features rather than managing individual destinations. As each feature evolves independently, the root navigation remains almost unchanged. And that’s exactly where you want the complexity to live — inside the feature that owns it, not at the application’s entry point. In the second half of this article, we’ll see why this pattern works particularly well with feature modules, when it makes sense to extract a feature, and why thinking in features instead of screens leads to a cleaner Navigation 3 architecture. A Natural Fit for Feature Modules This approach becomes even more valuable in modular applications. Instead of scattering navigation definitions across the app module, each feature can own its own screens and the navigation entries that belong to them. A typical project structure might look like this: feature-auth ├── LoginScreen ├── SignupScreen └── authFeature() feature-settings ├── SettingsScreen ├── LicenseScreen └── settingsFeature() feature-payment ├── CartScreen ├── CheckoutScreen └── paymentFeature() Each feature is responsible for exposing a single entry point. title: Properties and Backing Fields in Kotlin: A Complete Guide
excerpt: Every Kotlin class stores data. Whether it’s a user’s name, a product’s price, or a login state, that data is represented using properties… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Kotlin Beginners Kotlin Android Software Development Software Engineering Properties and Backing Fields in Kotlin: A Complete Guide Tech Dynasty 5 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share Every Kotlin class stores data. Whether it’s a user’s name, a product’s price, or a login state, that data is represented using properties . While properties look simple on the surface, Kotlin does a lot of work behind the scenes by automatically generating getters, setters, and backing fields. Press enter or click to view image in full size One of Kotlin’s biggest advantages over Java is that you rarely need to write boilerplate code for accessing or updating data. Instead, Kotlin provides a clean property syntax while still giving you full control when custom logic is required. In this article, you’ll learn what properties are, how getters and setters work, what backing fields are, when Kotlin creates them, and how they’re used in real Android applications. What Is a Property? A property is a variable that belongs to a class. It represents the state or data of an object. For example: class User { var name = "Janhvi" var age = 24 } Here: name age are properties of the User class. Creating an object: val user = User() println(user.name) println(user.age) Output: Janhvi 24 val vs var Kotlin provides two kinds of properties. Read-Only Property ( val ) val country = "India" A val property can be assigned only once. country = "USA" This produces a compilation error. Use val whenever the value should never change. Mutable Property ( var ) var city = "Delhi" city = "Bangalore" A var property can be updated at any time. Choose var only when mutability is required. How Kotlin Properties Work Consider the following property: var age = 24 Although it looks like a simple variable, Kotlin automatically generates: A getter A setter A backing field Conceptually, Kotlin creates something similar to: private var field = 24 fun getAge(): Int = field fun setAge(value: Int) { field = value } Unlike Java, you don’t have to write this boilerplate yourself. Default Getter and Setter Every mutable property automatically gets a getter and setter. class Student { var marks = 80 } Usage: val student = Student() student.marks = 95 println(student.marks) Behind the scenes, Kotlin calls: setMarks(95) getMarks() The syntax remains clean while preserving encapsulation. Custom Getters Sometimes a property’s value should be computed instead of stored. Example: class Rectangle( val width: Int, val height: Int ) { val area: Int get() = width * height } Usage: val rectangle = Rectangle(10, 5) println(rectangle.area) Output: 50 Notice that area isn't stored anywhere—it is calculated every time it's accessed. Custom Setters A setter allows you to validate or modify incoming values before storing them. Example: class Employee { var salary = 0 set(value) { field = if (value >= 0) value else 0 } } Usage: val employee = Employee() employee.salary = -5000 println(employee.salary) Output: 0 The setter prevents invalid values from being stored. What Is a Backing Field? A backing field is the hidden variable that actually stores a property’s value. You never declare it yourself. Kotlin creates it automatically whenever it’s needed. Inside getters and setters, it is accessed using the special keyword: field Example: var name = "Alex" set(value) { field = value.trim() } Here: value is the new value being assigned. field refers to the property's hidden storage. Why Use field ? Consider this setter: var username = "" set(value) { field = value.uppercase() } Usage: username = "janhvi" println(username) Output: JANHVI Without field , assigning directly to username inside its own setter would recursively call the setter, causing a stack overflow. The field keyword avoids that recursion. When Does Kotlin Create a Backing Field? A backing field is generated only when the property needs storage. It is created when: The property has a default getter or setter. A custom getter or setter uses field . Example: var age = 20 A backing field is created. But for a computed property: val area: Int get() = width * height No backing field is generated because the value is calculated dynamically. Read-Only Computed Properties Computed properties are useful when a value depends on other properties. class Circle( val radius: Double ) { val area: Double get() = 3.14 * radius * radius } Every access recalculates the area. Private Setter Sometimes you want a property to be readable from anywhere but modifiable only within the class. class Counter { var count = 0 private set fun increment() { count++ } } Usage: val counter = Counter() counter.increment() println(counter.count) External code can read count but cannot modify it directly. Late Initialization ( lateinit ) Sometimes a property cannot be initialized immediately. lateinit var username: String Later: username = "Janhvi" This is commonly used for: Dependency Injection Android Views View Binding Test setup lateinit can only be used with mutable ( var ) non-null reference types. Real-World Android Examples Form Validation var email = "" set(value) { field = value.trim() } Leading and trailing spaces are automatically removed. Product Price var price = 0.0 set(value) { require(value >= 0) field = value } Negative prices are prevented. User Score class Player( var wins: Int, var losses: Int ) { val totalMatches get() = wins + losses } totalMatches is always calculated from the latest values. Best Practices When working with Kotlin properties: Prefer val over var whenever possible. Use custom getters for computed values. Use custom setters for validation and formatting. Access the backing field using field inside getters and setters. Avoid expensive computations inside getters if they are called frequently. Keep setters simple and focused on validation or transformation. Use a private setter when only the class should modify a property. Following these practices helps create predictable, maintainable, and encapsulated classes

title: Android Passwordless Authentication: Implementing Passkeys with MVVM
excerpt: Passkeys are the modern, more secure alternative to passwords. Based on the FIDO2/WebAuthn standard, they allow users to sign in to apps… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Passwordless Passwordless Login Passkey Android Android Passwordless Authentication: Implementing Passkeys with MVVM Rajendrakumar Dabhi 3 min read · 5 hours ago -- Listen Share Passkeys are the modern, more secure alternative to passwords. Based on the FIDO2/WebAuthn standard, they allow users to sign in to apps and websites using their device’s screen lock (fingerprint, face, or PIN). Unlike passwords, passkeys are unique to every account and never leave the user’s device. In this guide, we’ll walk through implementing Passkey authentication in Android using the Credential Manager API and MVVM architecture. Press enter or click to view image in full size 🏗️ High-Level Design (HLD) Passkey authentication involves a two-step handshake between the app and the backend server for both registration and login. Passkey Authentication Flow Diagram: Press enter or click to view image in full size 🛠️ Implementation Steps 1. Add Dependencies Add the Credential Manager and Play Services Auth libraries to your build.gradle.kts: dependencies { implementation("androidx.credentials:credentials:1.5.0") implementation("androidx.credentials:credentials-play-services-auth:1.5.0") implementation("com.google.android.libraries.identity.googleid:googleid:1.1.1") } 2. The Passkey Authenticator Logic The PasskeyAuthenticator encapsulates the CredentialManager calls. It handles the JSON interaction required for FIDO2. class PasskeyAuthenticator(context: Context) { private val credentialManager = CredentialManager.create(context) suspend fun registerPasskey(activity: FragmentActivity, requestJson: String): Result<CreateCredentialResponse> { return try { val request = CreatePublicKeyCredentialRequest(requestJson) val result = credentialManager.createCredential(activity, request) Result.success(result) } catch (e: CreateCredentialException) { Result.failure(e) } } suspend fun loginWithPasskey(activity: FragmentActivity, requestJson: String): Result<GetCredentialResponse> { return try { val option = GetPublicKeyCredentialOption(requestJson) val request = GetCredentialRequest(listOf(option)) val result = credentialManager.getCredential(activity, request) Result.success(result) } catch (e: GetCredentialException) { Result.failure(e) } } } 3. ViewModel Integration (MVVM) The ViewModel handles the state transition and communicates with the backend to fetch challenges. sealed class PasskeyUiState { object Idle : PasskeyUiState() object Loading : PasskeyUiState() data class Success(val msg: String) : PasskeyUiState() data class Error(val error: String) : PasskeyUiState() } class PasskeyViewModel(private val authenticator: PasskeyAuthenticator) : ViewModel() { private val _uiState = MutableStateFlow<PasskeyUiState>(PasskeyUiState.Idle) val uiState: StateFlow<PasskeyUiState> = _uiState.asStateFlow() fun login(activity: FragmentActivity) { viewModelScope.launch { _uiState.value = PasskeyUiState.Loading // 1. Fetch challenge from your backend val challengeJson = repository.getLoginChallenge() // 2. Trigger Credential Manager val result = authenticator.loginWithPasskey(activity, challengeJson) // 3. Verify assertion with backend result.onSuccess { repository.verifyLoginAssertion(it) _uiState.value = PasskeyUiState.Success("Welcome back!") }.onFailure { _uiState.value = PasskeyUiState.Error(it.message ?: "Login failed") } } } } 4. UI with Jetpack Compose @Composable fun PasskeyScreen(viewModel: PasskeyViewModel) { val uiState by viewModel.uiState.collectAsState() Card(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth().padding(16.dp)) { Column(modifier = Modifier.padding(24.dp)) { Text("Passkey Authentication", style = MaterialTheme.typography.headlineSmall) Spacer(modifier = Modifier.height(16.dp)) Button( onClick = { viewModel.login(activity) }, enabled = uiState !is PasskeyUiState.Loading ) { Text("Sign in with Passkey") } } } } 🔐 Why Passkeys are Better 1.Phishing Resistant: Passkeys are bound to the domain (RP ID). A user cannot accidentally “type” their passkey into a fake website. 2. No More Passwords: Users don’t need to remember anything. They use the same biometric flow they use to unlock their phone. 3 .Sync-able: Passkeys are backed up to the cloud (e.g., Google Password Manager) and work across all the user’s Android devices. 🚀 Conclusion The shift towards a passwordless world is happening now. By integrating Passkeys into your Android app, you provide a world-class sign-in experience that is faster, easier, and significantly more secure than traditional credentials. Start building the passwordless future today! 🔑🚀

title: Secure Biometric Authentication in Android: The Complete Guide (MVVM)
excerpt: In the era of modern mobile applications, user experience and security must go hand in hand. Biometric Authentication (Fingerprint, Face… Continue reading on Medium »
content: Secure Biometric Authentication in Android: The Complete Guide (MVVM) Rajendrakumar Dabhi 3 min read · 1 day ago -- Listen Share In the era of modern mobile applications, user experience and security must go hand in hand. Biometric Authentication (Fingerprint, Face, and Iris) has become the gold standard for providing quick yet highly secure access to sensitive information. In this post, we will explore how to implement a production-ready Biometric Login flow in Android using the MVVM architecture and best security practices. Press enter or click to view image in full size 🏗️ High-Level Design (HLD) A common mistake is to treat biometric success as a simple “true/false” check. For a truly secure system, the authentication must be cryptographically verified by your backend server. Authentication Flow Diagram Press enter or click to view image in full size 🛠️ Implementation Steps Add Dependencies & Permissions First, add the Biometric library to your build.gradle.kts: dependencies { implementation("androidx.biometric:biometric-ktx:1.2.0-alpha05") } And add the permission to your AndroidManifest.xml: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.USE_BIOMETRIC" /> 2. The Authenticator Logic (The “How”) We encapsulate the BiometricPrompt logic in a dedicated class. This class handles the system dialog and callbacks. class BiometricAuthenticator(private val context: Context) { fun isBiometricAvailable(): Boolean { val biometricManager = BiometricManager.from(context) return biometricManager.canAuthenticate( BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG ) == BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_SUCCESS } fun promptBiometricAuth( activity: FragmentActivity, onSuccess: (BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult) -> Unit, onError: (Int, CharSequence) -> Unit ) { val executor = ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(activity) val biometricPrompt = BiometricPrompt(activity, executor, object : BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback() { override fun onAuthenticationSucceeded(result: BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult) { onSuccess(result) } // ... handle onAuthenticationError and onAuthenticationFailed }) val promptInfo = BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder() .setTitle("Biometric Login") .setSubtitle("Sign in using your biometrics") .setNegativeButtonText("Use Password") .build() biometricPrompt.authenticate(promptInfo) } } 3. Managing State with ViewModel Following MVVM, the ViewModel manages the authentication state (Idle, Loading, Success, Error) and ensures the UI remains reactive. sealed class AuthState { object Idle : AuthState() object Loading : AuthState() data class Success(val message: String) : AuthState() data class Error(val message: String) : AuthState() } class AuthViewModel(private val authenticator: BiometricAuthenticator) : ViewModel() { private val _authState = MutableStateFlow<AuthState>(AuthState.Idle) val authState: StateFlow<AuthState> = _authState.asStateFlow() fun authenticate(activity: FragmentActivity) { _authState.value = AuthState.Loading authenticator.promptBiometricAuth(activity, onSuccess = { result -> // Production: Use result.cryptoObject to sign a backend challenge _authState.value = AuthState.Success("Securely Authenticated!") }, onError = { code, msg -> _authState.value = AuthState.Error(msg.toString()) } ) } } 4. The User Interface (Jetpack Compose) Using Jetpack Compose, we create a clean UI that observes the ViewModel state. @Composable fun LoginScreen(viewModel: AuthViewModel) { val state by viewModel.authState.collectAsState() Column(horizontalAlignment = Alignment.CenterHorizontally) { when (state) { is AuthState.Loading -> CircularProgressIndicator() is AuthState.Success -> Icon(Icons.Default.CheckCircle, tint = Color.Green) is AuthState.Error -> Text("Error: ${(state as AuthState.Error).message}") else -> Text("Please Authenticate") } Button(onClick = { viewModel.authenticate(activity) }) { Text("Login with Fingerprint") } } } 🔐 Secure Backend Verification For maximum security, always use CryptoObject. 1.Generate a KeyPair in the Android Keystore with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true). 2.When onAuthenticationSucceeded is called, it means the private key is now “unlocked” for a short window. 3.Sign a Server Challenge with that private key. 4.Send the signature to your backend. 5.The backend verifies it using the public key you registered during the user’s initial setup. This ensures that even if a device is rooted, the biometric success cannot be “faked” because the private key never leaves the secure hardware. 🚀 Conclusion Biometric authentication is more than just a convenience feature; it’s a powerful tool in your security arsenal. By using androidx.biometric with a proper MVVM architecture and cryptographic signing, you provide your users with a login experience that is both seamless and incredibly secure. Happy Coding! 🔒📱

content: Smartphones Buying Guide Consumer Technology Android Tech 7 Mistakes People Make When Buying Smartphones Regular Product Review 3 min read · 1 day ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Buying a new smartphone should be exciting, but for many people it ends with disappointment. A phone may look impressive in advertisements or on a store shelf, yet fail to meet everyday expectations after a few weeks of use. Many buyers focus on flashy marketing, camera megapixels, or limited-time discounts while ignoring the features that actually affect daily performance. As a result, they spend more money than necessary or purchase a device that doesn’t fit their needs. Here are seven of the most common mistakes people make when buying a smartphone — and how you can avoid them. 1. Buying Based Only on Brand Name A well-known brand does not automatically mean the best value. Every manufacturer offers entry-level, mid-range, and flagship devices. Two phones from the same company can deliver completely different experiences. Instead of buying because of the logo, compare: Processor Display quality Battery life Camera performance Software support Build quality Always compare specifications before making a decision. 2. Ignoring the Processor The processor is the heart of every smartphone. Many buyers only look at RAM or storage, but the chipset has a much bigger impact on: Speed Gaming performance Battery efficiency Camera processing Long-term usability A powerful processor will often outperform a phone with more RAM but a weaker chipset. 3. Paying Too Much Attention to Camera Megapixels More megapixels do not guarantee better photos. Image quality depends on many factors, including: Sensor size Lens quality Image processing Optical stabilization Low-light performance Before buying, check real-world camera samples instead of relying only on marketing numbers. 4. Choosing the Wrong Storage Capacity Storage fills up faster than most people expect. Photos, videos, apps, games, and software updates quickly consume available space. General recommendations: 128GB for most users 256GB for heavy users 512GB or higher for content creators Choosing too little storage often leads to frustration later. 5. Overlooking Software Updates Software support is just as important as hardware. Phones with longer update commitments typically offer: Better security New Android features Improved performance Longer resale value A device that receives updates for several years is usually a smarter long-term investment. 6. Ignoring Battery Life Battery capacity alone doesn’t tell the whole story. A phone with a larger battery may still perform worse if the processor and software are inefficient. Consider: Real-world screen-on time Charging speed Wireless charging support Battery optimization Reading long-term user reviews can provide valuable insight into daily battery performance. 7. Not Reading Trusted Reviews Marketing materials rarely mention weaknesses. Independent reviews reveal important details such as: Heating issues Display quality Camera consistency Speaker performance Software bugs Long-term reliability Always compare several trusted review sources before making your final decision. Final Thoughts Buying the right smartphone isn’t about purchasing the most expensive model — it’s about choosing the device that best fits your needs and budget. By avoiding these seven common mistakes, you can make a smarter purchase and enjoy your smartphone for years to come. content: From Script to Finished Video: A Complete Guide to Teleprompter Automatic Teleprompter Automatic 11 min read · 2 days ago -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size How to prepare scripts, choose the right scrolling mode, record video or audio, stream live, edit the result, and keep your projects synchronized across iPhone, Android, and the web Disclosure: Teleprompter Automatic is my product. Memorizing a script is rarely the only challenge when recording a video. You also have to maintain eye contact, speak at a natural pace, control the camera, monitor the microphone, start recording without an awkward pause, and turn the result into a publishable video. Teleprompter Automatic is designed to bring these steps into one connected workflow. It is available for iPhone and iPad, Android devices, and the web. The mobile apps provide the complete camera, audio, reader, editing, and export experience, while the web version is especially useful for writing scripts, rehearsing, managing cloud content, recording with a compatible webcam, and remotely controlling a mounted phone. ( Teleprompter Automatic ) Insert the feature overview image here Teleprompter Automatic combines script preparation, four scrolling modes, video and audio recording, editing, remote control, and cloud synchronization. Feature availability may depend on the device, operating system, browser capabilities, permissions, account state, and subscription. The features by platform page provides a practical comparison of the iPhone, Android, and web workflows. ( Teleprompter Automatic ) One product, three ways to work The best device for preparing a script is not always the best device for recording it. On the web , you have a physical keyboard and a larger screen, making it easier to write, import, organize, and rehearse longer scripts. You can open the reader in fullscreen mode, adjust the text, mirror it, set a countdown, and record from a webcam when the browser supports the required media features. On iPhone and iPad , the script, camera, subtitles, editing tools, cloud sync, Apple Watch controls, and export workflow can stay inside one mobile setup. On Android , you can manage scripts and folders, import documents, choose different reader modes, use speech-recognition scrolling, record through the phone camera, edit the result, and synchronize supported content. Sign in with the same account on each platform when you want scripts, folders, subscriptions, devices, and cloud-connected projects to remain consistent. ( Teleprompter Automatic ) Start with a script that is comfortable to say aloud A teleprompter cannot make an overly complicated script sound natural. The first step is therefore not choosing a camera setting. It is preparing text that works as speech. Inside Teleprompter Automatic, you can create a blank script, paste existing text, import supported files, and organize related scripts into folders. Folders are particularly useful when you record for several clients, courses, channels, campaigns, or recurring content formats. For easier reading, keep paragraphs short and give each paragraph one clear idea. Put names, numbers, product claims, and calls to action on separate lines when they need special attention. When importing a PDF, use a document with selectable text whenever possible. Scanned PDFs may need OCR before import, and imported documents should be checked for page numbers, headers, footers, and unnecessary line breaks. The detailed process is covered in the script creation and import guide . ( Teleprompter Automatic ) Create a first draft with AI When you know what the video should communicate but do not know how to begin, the AI Video Script Generator can turn a rough idea into a spoken starter script. A useful prompt should include: the intended audience; the purpose and format of the video; the approximate duration; the main message or offer; the action the viewer should take. The generated text should still be read aloud, edited, and fact-checked. AI is useful for structure, but product claims, prices, results, legal wording, and customer promises should always be verified before publication. A generated script can then be rehearsed on the web and saved for recording in the iOS or Android app. ( Teleprompter Automatic ) Adjust the appearance of the text Before recording, you can adjust text size, line spacing, alignment, capitalization, colors, and the position of the reading area. The goal is not to fit as many words as possible on the screen. The goal is to keep your eyes relaxed and close to the camera. Teleprompter Automatic also supports horizontal and vertical text mirroring. This is important when using beam-splitter glass, a reflected teleprompter rig, or an external display that reverses the image. Text mirroring changes only what the speaker sees; it is separate from mirroring the recorded video. The mirroring guide explains the difference. ( Teleprompter Automatic ) Choose the scrolling mode that matches the recording There is no single scrolling mode that works for every speaker and every project. Teleprompter Automatic provides four different approaches. Fixed speed Fixed-speed scrolling moves the script continuously at one predictable pace. It is a good choice for noisy environments, product demonstrations, silent practice, recordings with background music, or any situation in which speech recognition may be unreliable. Start at a moderate speed, read the opening paragraph aloud, and adjust until you no longer feel that you are chasing the text or waiting for it. Timed scrolling Timed scrolling calculates the pace from a target duration. This mode is useful for a 30-second advertisement, a one-minute update, a timed presentation segment, or any video that must stay close to a specific length.
